title: Response Strategy Pocket Guide — Field Ops (WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, actionable pocket guide for field sellers and solutions engineers to run short demo conversations and handle rapid objections during discovery and technical calls. Focus is on: 1) quick explanation of Redwood differentiation around serving, 2) rapid fallback & SLA narratives, 3) two-minute technical answers for common infra questions, 4) a small checklist for canary/rollout promises.

Audience:
- AE/SEs doing discovery with platform, infra, product teams
- SDRs prepping for discovery handoff
- Customer engineers during quick triage calls

Use guidance (how to carry this doc into a call):
- Keep it pocket-sized: open to the "Quick rebuttals" section when challenged on cost or latency.
- Use the "Route decisions" mini-diagram (verbal) to explain fallback: hosted -> dedicated -> private. Emphasize same API and predictable behavior.
- When asked about privacy/regulation: point to Private deployment + KMS/HSM bullet and offer to share the security package (link above).

Top-line win themes (elevator, 30s):
- "Same dev experience across hosted, reserved, and private deployments — ship once, run anywhere.
- Predictable economics: dedicated capacity and batching controls let you trade latency for cost with measurable unit economics.
- Reliability-first: automated fallbacks and canary rollouts keep production features up during model or capacity problems."

Quick metrics to cite (rounded for verbal use):
- Typical 1k-token gen latency (p95) on hosted: ~120–220ms per token depending on model class (say: 150ms median for 13B quantized in region).
- Dedicated SLOs: configurable p95 targets with contractual uptime (example plan: 99.5% availability).
- Embeddings throughput: batched embeddings can reduce billed cost by up to 3x for large batch jobs.
(Note: always caveat: "customer workload dependent — we can run quick evals to validate")

Quick rebuttals / objection scripts:
- "We can self-host cheaper":
  + "If you have an infra team and spare cycles it might be cheaper at huge scale — but you’ll need to invest in runtime optimizations (KV cache, batching, low-latency kernels), ops for fallbacks, and ongoing model compatibility work. Redwood offloads that — especially helpful for teams shipping product features quickly."
- "Latency is critical for us":
  + "We have dedicated capacity with configurable autoscale and burst. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated or Private with pinned model variants; we also ship kernel/profile recommendations based on your seq-length distribution."
- "What if an upstream model regresses?":
  + "We decouple model rollouts from API surface. Canary rollouts, A/B routing, and automatic fallback to vetted variants keep your feature live while we resolve regressions."
- "How do you save costs vs. always calling a large model?":
  + "Routing policies let you use cheaper model variants for routine requests and promote to larger models only for high-value requests. Combined with prefix caching and batching we usually see 30–60% per-token cost reduction in mixed workloads."

Technical one-liners (for SEs to say quickly):
- "Serving runtime uses kernel selection and quantization-aware paths to squeeze more throughput from GPUs without changing your prompts."
- "We support KV prefix caching — it’s transparent to the app and can drastically reduce repeat-token costs for chat-like workloads."
- "Routing policies are policy-as-code: route by latency budget, cost cap, or accuracy label."

Rapid demo script (3 min):
1) Start: “We’ll show a single API call that runs across hosted + fallback model.” (30s)
2) Show low-latency response (local demo/recording) and point out p95 number (30s)
3) Trigger a simulated capacity constraint -> show automatic fallback to a compatible variant (30s)
4) Show routing rule toggle in Console (canary -> full) (30s)
5) Close with KPI ask: "What throughput and latency are you targeting?" (30s)

Checklist for promise commitments (shareable after-call):
- Ask for throughput profile (qps, burst size, average tokens per request)
- Note model family preference / regulatory constraints (e.g., no internet-connected models)
- Confirm whether data residency matters (region requirement)
- Agree on next step: quick eval (sample workload + perf test) or architecture deep-dive session

Handy links to reference (call-ready):
- Security & private deployment package (send after call): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/security-private
- Quick perf eval template (send to engineering): JIRA:INF-3248
- Console demo recording (internal): https://drive.redwood.ai/console-demo/short-recording

Open questions / placeholders (action items for G2M):
- Need a one-click demo recording for the Dedicated fallback sequence (ask infra for a short clip). -> action: Marco to coordinate (ETA 2w).
- Clarify up-to-date p95 numbers per model family for public speaking lines (Priya to pull recent bench).
- Create a 1-page PDF version for AE Slack share (size constraint: <100KB).

Notes to self / rough phrasing (non-customer facing):
- Keep numbers conservative. Don’t promise specific token latency unless we’ve validated on customer’s sample.
- Use "predictable economics" framing vs. "cheaper" — avoids direct price war.
- Emphasize "same API across environments" — big win for platform teams.

Revision history (quick):
- 2025-01-18: initial draft, field-tested in two discovery calls.
- 2025-01-28: added rapid demo script + checklist.
- 2025-02-06: updated linked artifacts and open action items.

Slack shorthand / quick copy snippets (paste into DM):
- "We offer dedicated GPU pools with SLA-backed p95s + automatic model fallbacks. Can I set up a 30-min perf eval with your infra team?"
- "If you care about consistent API and predictable unit economics across hosted and on-prem, Redwood is built for the handoff from prototype to product."

End — this is a living doc. Add field-tested lines back into the ‘call phrases’ section as we validate them in real calls.
